utility.notes: LES is a municipally-owned electric utility serving Lincoln, Nebraska, Nebraska's capital and second-largest city. Omaha Public Power District (OPPD) and the City of Omaha were confirmed genuinely blocked earlier in this marathon. This record pivots to Lincoln and its own separate public-power utility instead.

value.name: Lincoln Electric System (LES)
value.notes: Recorded as both the distribution and generation utility. Nebraska is the only U.S. state served at retail entirely by consumer-owned electric utilities (public power districts, cooperatives, and municipalities) — there are no investor-owned utilities in Nebraska.

county.notes: Lincoln, Nebraska's capital, is the seat of Lancaster County.

value.program_or_pathway: City of Lincoln's streamlined residential solar PV permit review (systems 25 kW AC or less on single-family or duplex rooftops), combined with LES's net metering program under Nebraska's statewide Net Metering statute (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 70-2001 to 70-2005, enacted 2009 via LB 436).
other_conditions: A 'qualified facility' under Nebraska's statewide statute must have a rated capacity at or below 25 kilowatts, be located on and controlled by the customer-generator's own premises, interconnect and operate in parallel with the local distribution system, and be equipped to automatically isolate itself during a power outage.

Net metering credits the customer-generator at the full retail rate for each kWh that offsets their own electricity use during a billing period; any net excess generation beyond the customer's own usage is instead compensated at the local utility's avoided cost of electric supply (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 70-2002(6)).

The customer-generator's minimum monthly fee may not exceed that charged to other customers in the same rate class, and no additional standby, capacity, demand, interconnection, safety-testing, or liability-insurance requirement beyond the statute's own standards may be imposed.

A local distribution utility is not required to accept additional net-metering customers once the combined capacity of all its net-metering customer-generators reaches 1% of its average aggregate customer monthly peak demand forecast for that calendar year — though a utility may voluntarily offer net metering above this cap or for systems above 25 kW at its own discretion.
